In the rest of this review we will work with the Kauffman bracket version of the Jones polynomial. The
whole purpose of section 2 is to explain what knot is and how the bracket polynomial can be computed,
for example, using the skein relation. We will need this calculus for quantum mechanical applications.
Let us summarize the main steps:
• Draw the knot (link) diagram;
• Choose a crossing, apply the skein relation by replacing the diagram by a pair of new diagrams
with the crossing modified according to skein relation (25);
• Repeat the procedure for the next crossing for each of the generated diagrams until the diagrams
are nothing but a collection of nested nonintersecting circles;
• replace each circle by factor d = −A2 −A−2.

First, let us discuss the property of entanglement entropy called subadditivity. Let us assume that in a
given quantum system one can separate a subsystem A and another subsystem B. Then the subadditivity
of the entropy is the statement that the entropy of the union of A and B is not greater than the sum of
entropies of A and B:
SvN(A + B) ≤SvN(A) + SvN(B) .
Instead of trying to interpret this inequality right away, let us first produce its topological analog.
Consider a generic state in the connectome limit. Note that the union A + B does not necessarily
represent the whole system, so there is also a complement A + B = C. Thus, a generic state will have the
form shown in figure 3 (left), where lines between subsystems A, B and C illustrate generic correlations
between them.
In the limit that we are applying, the correlations are quantified by the number of
connections. Let NA, NB and NC be the numbers of connections of the respective subsystems to the
remaining parts. Let ℓAB be the number of connections exclusively between A and B. Then a simple
relation holds:
NA + NB = NC + 2ℓAB ≥NC .
Since the entanglement entropy is proportional to the number of connections, with log 2 coefficient, the
subadditivity property (157) follows.
With the connectivity quantification of entanglement it is not hard to give an interpretation to the
subadditivity. The correlation of A and B with the rest of the system cannot exceed the the amount of
correlations in A and B taken together, simply because there might exist correlations between A and B.
The amount of correlation between A and B, in this case, is
ℓAB = (NA + NB −NC)/2 .
This is the topological version of what is known in Information Theory as mutual information I(A, B),
I(A, B) := SvN(A) + SvN(B) −SvN(A + B) .
If the system A + B does not have a complement (isolated) then SvN(A + B) = 0, SvN(A) = SvN(B) and
mutual information is essentially the same as the entanglement entropy.
Another very-well known inequality is strong subadditivity. It is formulated for three subsystems A,
B and C. The inequality states
SvN(A + B + C) + SvN(B) ≤SvN(A + B) + SvN(B + C) .
In terms of connectivity this inequality can be proven using the diagram shown in figure 3 (right), where
D = A + B + C. Denoting the number of connections as in the previous case one finds that
ND = NA+B + NB+C −2ℓAC −NB ≤NA+B + NB+C −NB ,

Strong subadditivity is notoriously difficult to prove in general [104], but for the special class of states
that we consider here it comes almost for free. Many more known inequalities can be tested in this way
and some new ones can be designed [86,102]. It is important to keep in mind that in generic quantum
states the relations derived in the connectome limit might not hold. Since it is an open question whether
and how much the connectome relations may be violated, we will discuss some possibilities in section 6.
Quantum Algorithms
As another set of applications of the topological visualization of quantum mechanics let us consider
a pair of basic quantum algorithms. Quantum algorithms exploiting quantum correlations should be
the most natural target for such a study. The example of the EPR pair puzzles us with the apparent
instantaneity of interactions between causally separated particles.
Quantum teleportation is a basic
algorithm that capitalizes on this effect making an arbitrary state “instantaneously” available in a distant
lab. Superdense coding is another example. We will discuss topological realization of both algorithms
elucidating their inherent similarity.
Quantum Teleportation

Let us also mention another subtlety highlighted by protocol (170). Note that sections of the diagram
(vertical gray lines) involve a Hilbert space of eight points, rather than a tensor product of two four-point
Hilbert spaces. This means that the initial two-qubit state is embedded into a large Hilbert space (in
general, of dimension 14). This is not a problem as long as the result of the protocol is restricted to
belong to the four-dimensional two-qubit subspace. It is instructive to check what would happen if a
tensor product of two four-point spaces were used.
First, application of a nonlocal, two-qubit, operation would result in a topological defect – a hole in

Such a whole would obstruct realization of the necessary final states: One would not be able to freely move
the lines around. Second, the operator, of the type appearing in (172) would not in general be unitary,
for a similar reason. Figure 5 illustrates the fact that concatenating the operator and its Hermitian
conjugate will not in general produce the identity due to a topological defect.
These comments complement a more naive version of this topological protocol considered in [102].
